analysis.one_liner: Registers tax preparers and refund loan providers, caps loan fees, and funds free tax help and bank accounts for low-income taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2003 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required tax preparers and refund anticipation loan providers to register with the Treasury and follow rules of conduct, and directed the Treasury to set limits on 'reasonable fees and interest rates' for refund loans. It would have shut off the IRS Debt Indicator program — the government data feed that told lenders a taxpayer's refund was coming, making the loans nearly risk-free — and pushed free electronic filing so refunds arrive fast without a loan. It also authorized about $10 million a year in grants to help unbanked taxpayers open accounts at federally insured banks or credit unions, and up to another $10 million a year in matching grants for low-cost tax clinics serving people at or below 250 percent of the poverty line. The bill's own findings put the problem in dollar terms: nearly half of the roughly $30 billion in Earned Income Tax Credit was being refunded through anticipation loans, and about $1.75 billion meant for low-income families was going to commercial preparers and affiliated banks as fees for tax prep, e-filing, and high-cost loans, some carrying rates between 97.4 percent and more than 2000 percent.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income taxpayers, especially the roughly 40 million unbanked Americans named in the bill's findings and the families claiming the Earned Income Tax Credit. Registered preparers and loan providers would face conduct rules and fee limits, the IRS debt indicator that powers refund anticipation loans would be terminated, free electronic filing and direct-deposit accounts would get refunds into people's hands faster without a loan or a check casher, and grant-funded clinics and mobile tax offices would provide free or nominal-cost return preparation, including on Indian reservations.

how_it_helps.text: It would require registration of every tax preparer and refund anticipation loan provider and impose a $500 fine per incident for anyone working without a registration number, creating a named, trackable counterparty for abuses.
It directs the Treasury to write rules on 'reasonable fees and interest rates' for refund anticipation loans, which the bill's findings note ran between 97.4 percent and more than 2000 percent.
It would terminate the IRS Debt Indicator program, which lenders used to confirm that a refund would exist before making a loan — removing the government data that made the lending machine work.

It would fund demonstration grants to help unbanked low- and moderate-income taxpayers open accounts at federally insured banks or credit unions, so refunds arrive by direct deposit instead of through a loan or a check casher; the bill's findings note check-cashing fees already cost EITC recipients about $130 million a year.

It would give matching grants, up to $10 million a year, to low-cost tax return clinics serving low-income taxpayers, and set up mobile tax filing offices in high EITC-claiming communities, including at least one on or near an Indian reservation.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation chains and refund anticipation loan providers, along with the national banks that fund those loans, would lose revenue from loan fees and paid e-filing; check-cashing services would lose EITC-related business. Small independent preparers would bear new registration and paperwork costs, and the Treasury would administer the programs at a cost of roughly $20 million a year in authorized spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Refund loan lenders and tax prep chains

drawbacks.text: Registration, conduct rules, and fee guidance for refund anticipation loan providers would impose new compliance costs on commercial tax preparers and their partner banks; the bill instructs the Secretary to minimize that burden, but small independent preparers could still face registration fees and paperwork.

The bill authorizes roughly $20 million a year in federal spending ($10 million for account-establishment grants and $10 million for low-income tax clinics), a recurring cost to taxpayers, though small relative to federal budgets.

A good-faith objection from the industry side: refund anticipation loans serve filers who want cash immediately and lack bank accounts; restricting fees and redirecting refunds to direct deposit could leave some borrowers with slower access to money in emergencies. The bill's answer is that a bank account plus faster electronic refunds removes the need for the loan, but that transition would depend on the outreach and grant programs actually reaching the unbanked.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs were modest and the bill itself tried to limit them: about $20 million a year in authorizations, capped clinic administration, a 6 percent cap on grant overhead, and instructions to the Treasury to keep the registration burden and paperwork light for small preparers [S3]. Against that, the bill's own findings put the money at stake at roughly $1.75 billion a year skimmed from the Earned Income Tax Credit through loan fees, filing fees, and check cashing [S3]. A fair objection is that regulation of refund anticipation loans, however designed, could push some borrowers toward other high-cost products if faster-cash needs go unmet; the bill's answer — direct deposit into free or low-cost accounts — was a partial fix that would have depended on outreach working. On the whole, a low-cost bill whose benefits to low-income filers would likely have outweighed the administrative burden by a wide margin.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and the Congress ended in January 2005 with no hearing, no vote, and no action of any kind after the referral [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Bingaman introduced the bill on March 21, 2003, joined by Senator Daniel Akaka; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S5].

The complete action history contains exactly three entries — introduction, sponsor remarks, and the committee referral — with no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point in the 108th Congress.
The bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005; any bill not passed by both chambers before a Congress ends expires and must be reintroduced from scratch.

Because the bill never became law, refund anticipation loan providers and commercial preparers faced no new federal registration requirement, no fee and interest-rate guidance, and no termination of the IRS Debt Indicator program under this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The commercial tax preparation and refund anticipation loan industry is better off: it faced no new registration, no fee caps, and no loss of the IRS debt indicator, and the roughly $1.75 billion a year in fees drawn from Earned Income Tax Credit recipients under the old system continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Refund loan providers and commercial tax chains

for.name: Jeff Bingaman
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 21, 2003 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it; the bill received no action after referral for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll call to break down; the bill's only two Senate supporters were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee, where the bill sat, never acted on it.

industries.industry: Commercial tax preparation chains and refund anticipation loan lenders (and the national banks that funded the loans)
industries.note: The bill's own findings state that in 1999 nearly half of the $30 billion in Earned Income Tax Credit was refunded through refund anticipation loans and about $1.75 billion of the credit meant for low-income families was captured by commercial preparers and affiliated banks as fees. Registration, conduct rules, fee and interest-rate limits, termination of the IRS debt indicator, and free direct electronic filing would directly cut that revenue.

Roughly 45 percent of EITC recipients paid check-cashing fees, which the bill's findings put at $130 million a year. Helping filers open bank accounts and receive refunds by direct deposit would remove much of that business.

The grant program would pay to open federally insured accounts for unbanked taxpayers, bringing new deposit relationships to banks and credit unions at low fees. This helps the filer and the depository at the same time, which is why the bill pairs it with fee guidance rather than leaving it unregulated.

industries.industry: Nonprofit tax clinics and volunteer tax assistance programs (VITA)
industries.note: The bill would add up to $10 million a year in matching grants to expand low-cost return-preparation clinics and would fund a study on expanding VITA to reach more low-income taxpayers. Clinics charge no more than a nominal fee, so taxpayers gain free or cheap preparation.
